output.chapter_summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing a common function. The body has four main tissue types. Epithelial tissue covers and lines organs and cavities. Muscular tissue brings about movement. Neural tissue responds to stimuli. Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. Epithelial cells are tightly packed in a continuous sheet, with little cementing material and almost no intercellular space, and rest on a fibrous basement membrane. Some epithelial cells become gland cells, and inward folds form multicellular glands (glandular epithelium). By cell shape and number of layers, epithelia are simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar) or stratified (squamous, cuboidal, columnar), each with a characteristic location, structure and function. Muscle is of three types. Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striated, has one central nucleus and is involuntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is unstriated, has one central nucleus and is involuntary. Fig. 6.10 shows the connective tissues: blood cells (five WBC types, platelets, RBC), compact bone (Haversian canal, canaliculi), hyaline cartilage (chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix), areolar tissue (fibroblast, collagen and reticular fibres, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell) and adipose tissue (adipocytes with fat droplets). Neurons carry impulses from dendrites to the cell body, then along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips, which meet the next neuron's dendrites at a synapse.

concepts.name: Four basic types of animal tissue
concepts.core_explanation: The book says our body has mainly four tissue types, each defined by one job. Epithelial tissue provides covering or lining. Muscular tissue helps in movement. Neural tissue responds to stimuli. Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. Learn 'cover, move, respond, support' as the anchor: every later detail in the chapter is a sub-type of one of these four.

concepts.name: General features of epithelial tissue
concepts.core_explanation: Epithelium covers most organs and cavities and forms a barrier that keeps different body systems separate. To act as a barrier, its cells are tightly packed into a continuous sheet, with only a small amount of cementing material and almost no intercellular spaces, so substances cannot leak between cells. The whole sheet sits on an extracellular fibrous basement membrane, which separates it from the underlying tissue. Outside knowledge: epithelium has no blood vessels of its own and is nourished by diffusion from the tissue below.

concepts.name: Glandular epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Some epithelial cells become further specialised as gland cells that secrete substances at the epithelial surface. When a portion of the epithelial sheet folds inward, a multicellular gland is formed. This secretory epithelium is called glandular epithelium. Outside knowledge: a mucus-secreting goblet cell is a unicellular gland, while sweat and salivary glands are multicellular glands formed by such infolding.

concepts.name: Shapes of epithelial cells (Fig. 6.9)
concepts.core_explanation: Fig. 6.9 shows four epithelia. (a) Squamous is a single thin layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries. (b) Stratified squamous is many layers, with the flattest cells on top. (c) Cuboidal is a single layer of cube-like cells with round nuclei. (d) Columnar (ciliated) is a single layer of tall cells bearing hair-like cilia on the free surface. Naming rule: cell shape (squamous = flat, cuboidal = cube, columnar = tall) plus number of layers (simple = one, stratified = many).

concepts.name: Simple epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: Simple squamous is one layer of flat, irregular cells lining blood vessels, capillaries, lung air sacs and Bowman's capsule. It allows transport by diffusion where minimal protection is needed, because a thin layer means a short diffusion path. Simple cuboidal is one layer of short cylindrical cells lining kidney tubules and glandular ducts, and may carry microvilli as in the proximal convoluted tubule. It does absorption and secretion; microvilli increase surface area (outside). Simple columnar is one layer of tall, slender, often ciliated cells lining the digestive tract and upper respiratory tract. It does protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction, since cilia beat to push mucus one way.

concepts.name: Stratified epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: Stratified epithelia have several layers and are mainly protective. Stratified squamous lines the mouth and vagina. Its lower layer is columnar and metabolically active, dividing to produce new cells that are pushed upward, become flat and are sloughed off. This continuous renewal protects against abrasion. Stratified cuboidal has a cuboidal upper layer and lines the ducts of mammary, sweat and salivary glands, protecting them. Stratified columnar has a top layer of columnar cells over squamous, cuboidal or columnar cells, is found in the male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands, and does protection and secretion. Remember: a stratified epithelium is named after the shape of its top layer.

concepts.name: Three types of muscular tissue – comparison table
concepts.core_explanation: The book compares skeletal, cardiac and visceral (smooth) muscle on five parameters: location, function, appearance, control and cell drawing. Skeletal fibres are cylindrical, striped and have many edge nuclei. Cardiac cells are branched, striped and interlinked. Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with one central nucleus. Striations mark skeletal and cardiac muscle; voluntary control marks only skeletal muscle.

concepts.name: Skeletal muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Skeletal muscle is attached to the skeleton and is responsible for movement, heat production and posture. It is striated, multinucleated with eccentric (edge) nuclei, and its fibres run parallel. It is the only voluntary muscle. Outside knowledge: shivering is skeletal muscle contraction producing heat, and the many nuclei arise because each fibre forms by fusion of many cells.

concepts.name: Cardiac muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and pumps blood continuously throughout life. It is striated like skeletal muscle but has one central nucleus, and it is involuntary. Its cells are branched and interlinked (Fig. in p007-i2), so the heart contracts as a unit. It is the classic odd-one-out: striated but involuntary.

concepts.name: Visceral (smooth) muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Smooth muscle lies in the walls of the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels. It controls peristalsis, blood pressure (by narrowing or widening vessels), pupil size and the erection of hairs. It has no striations, one central nucleus and spindle-shaped cells, and is involuntary. Outside knowledge: hair erection ('goosebumps') is done by tiny arrector pili smooth muscles, and uterine smooth muscle contracts during childbirth.

concepts.name: Connective tissues – overview of Fig. 6.10
concepts.core_explanation: Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. Fig. 6.10 shows five examples: (a) blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue and (e) adipose tissue. Unlike epithelium, connective tissue cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix of ground substance and fibres (outside, standard). This matrix may be fluid (plasma in blood), rigid (bone), firm-flexible (cartilage) or loose (areolar).

concepts.name: Blood cells (Fig. 6.10a)
concepts.core_explanation: Panel (a) shows the different white blood corpuscles. Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte), eosinophil and basophil are granulocytes with granular cytoplasm and a dark-stained nucleus. Lymphocyte and monocyte are the other two WBCs. Platelets are small fragments, and the red blood corpuscle is a pale round disc. Outside knowledge: WBCs fight infection, platelets help clotting, and RBCs carry oxygen by haemoglobin. Mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus, which gives them a biconcave disc shape.

concepts.name: Compact bone (Fig. 6.10b)
concepts.core_explanation: Compact bone has concentric rings of hard matrix around a central Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels and nerve fibres. Fine canaliculi radiate from the bone cells (osteocytes) and hold their slender processes. Outside knowledge: because the matrix is hard and calcified, nutrients reach osteocytes through the Haversian canal and canaliculi, and each ring system is called a Haversian system (osteon).

concepts.name: Hyaline cartilage (Fig. 6.10c)
concepts.core_explanation: Hyaline cartilage consists of cartilage cells called chondrocytes, often in pairs, lying in a clear, glassy hyaline matrix. Outside knowledge: the matrix is firm yet flexible, and hyaline cartilage is found at the ends of long bones, the nose tip, the trachea rings and the larynx. It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.

concepts.name: Areolar tissue (Fig. 6.10d)
concepts.core_explanation: Areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue with thin branching reticular fibres and thick wavy collagen fibres. Its cells are the star-shaped fibroblast, the irregular macrophage, the rounded mast cell and the plasma cell. Outside knowledge: fibroblasts make the fibres, macrophages engulf microbes, mast cells release histamine, and plasma cells (from B lymphocytes) make antibodies. It lies under the skin and around organs, acting as packing and defence tissue.

concepts.name: Adipose tissue (Fig. 6.10e)
concepts.core_explanation: Adipose tissue is made of adipocytes (fat cells). Each is filled by a large fat droplet that pushes the small nucleus to the edge of the cell. Outside knowledge: it stores energy as fat, insulates the body under the skin and cushions organs such as the kidneys.

concepts.name: Structure of a neuron
concepts.core_explanation: A neuron has a central star-shaped cell body with a nucleus. Short branched dendrites receive signals, and one long axon carries the signal away from the cell body, ending in branched axon tips. The dendrites of one neuron receive input from the axon of the previous neuron. The neuron is the structural and functional unit of neural tissue, which responds to stimuli.

concepts.name: Impulse transmission and the synapse
concepts.core_explanation: A message moves in one direction: dendrites, then cell body, then axon (as an electrical signal), then axon tips, then a synapse, then the dendrites of the next neuron. The synapse is the junction between the axon tips of one neuron and the dendrites of the next. Outside knowledge: at the synapse the electrical signal is converted into a chemical signal (neurotransmitter), which is why impulses travel only one way.

Smooth muscle locations and functions (peristalsis, pupil, blood pressure, hair erection) appear in statement questions.

Haversian canal contents (blood vessels and nerves) and canaliculi with osteocytes are frequently tested structure facts.
The cells of areolar tissue (fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell) and their roles are often tested.

problems.problem: The map supplies a chapter summary but no reviewable notes explaining its scope decisions, reasons for outside additions, or uncertainties. In particular, the ambiguous diagram base and questionable epithelial-table wording are not acknowledged.
problems.fix: Add brief notes covering the unit's scope, key teaching questions, inclusion and sequencing decisions with reasons, and unresolved source ambiguities.

problems.problem: Outside knowledge is not consistently marked. Examples include the tissue definition in the summary, epithelial naming rules, the short-diffusion-path explanation, directional mucus transport, abrasion as the reason for renewal, cardiac coordination, granulocyte classification, and the neuron as the structural and functional unit of neural tissue. Relations also introduce outside classifications and biological connections without identifying their basis.
problems.fix: Separate page-supported statements from outside explanations consistently throughout the map, including relation notes and the summary where applicable. Retain correct additions, but label their basis explicitly.

problems.problem: The claim that tightly packed cells mean substances 'cannot leak between cells' is an incorrect absolute. Epithelial paracellular permeability varies; almost no visible intercellular space does not itself establish an impermeable seal.
problems.fix: Say that close packing and cell junctions create a selective barrier and restrict uncontrolled passage. Mark the junction/permeability explanation as outside knowledge and avoid claiming complete impermeability.

problems.where: C04 and C05; p003-i15 and p003-i20
problems.problem: The map presents cuboidal cells as cube-like in C04 but repeats 'short cylindrical cells' in C05 without resolving the conflict. This leaves the central shape-based classification internally inconsistent.
problems.fix: Preserve the table wording as a source statement, then explicitly clarify using standard outside knowledge that cuboidal cells are approximately as tall as they are wide; distinguish them from tall columnar cells.

problems.problem: The source's broad description of simple columnar epithelium as lining the digestive tract and upper respiratory tract, and being 'often ciliated', is repeated as an unqualified biological rule. Much of the conducting respiratory lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar, while typical intestinal absorptive columnar cells bear microvilli rather than motile cilia.
problems.fix: Identify the source statement explicitly and add a labelled standard clarification distinguishing non-ciliated absorptive columnar, ciliated columnar, and pseudostratified ciliated respiratory epithelium. Explain that microvilli increase surface area whereas motile cilia move material; ensure the exam-focus wording does not reinforce the conflation.

problems.problem: The statement that mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus, 'which gives them a biconcave disc shape', supplies an incorrect causal explanation. Enucleation alone does not determine biconcavity.
problems.fix: State separately that mature mammalian RBCs lack nuclei and are typically biconcave. If explaining shape, attribute its maintenance to membrane–cytoskeletal organisation, clearly marked as outside knowledge.

problems.problem: The map presents all synaptic transmission as electrical-to-chemical conversion and says this conversion is why impulses travel only one way. Chemical conversion alone does not explain directionality, and electrical synapses also exist.
problems.fix: Describe the usual chemical synapse as an explicitly labelled outside explanation: presynaptic terminals release neurotransmitter, which acts on postsynaptic receptors and can initiate a new electrical response. Attribute typical one-way transmission to this functional asymmetry, and avoid making the description universal to all synapses or neural signalling.

problems.where: C09, explanation of cardiac branching and interlinking
problems.problem: The statement that cells are branched and interlinked 'so the heart contracts as a unit' makes anatomical branching alone the explanation for coordination and can suggest that the whole heart contracts simultaneously.
problems.fix: Keep the diagram-supported branching description. If adding mechanism, label as outside knowledge that electrical coupling through gap junctions helps coordinate cardiac cells, with atrial and ventricular activity occurring in an organised sequence.

problems.problem: The stratified cuboidal explanation retains the cuboidal upper layer but omits the row's qualification that other layers may be cuboidal or other cell types. That qualification is teachable and directly supports the top-layer naming rule.
problems.fix: Restore the statement about possible underlying cell shapes and connect it explicitly to classification by the superficial layer.

problems.problem: The figure's unlabelled blue base is omitted entirely, including the supplied uncertainty about whether it represents basement membrane or underlying tissue. This leaves a visible diagram feature unexplained.
problems.fix: Acknowledge the base in the diagram explanation and retain its uncertain identification. Connect it cautiously to C02 without claiming that the figure labels it as basement membrane.

problems.problem: The map generalises the illustrated star-shaped cell body into a universal neuron description: 'A neuron has a central star-shaped cell body'. Neuronal cell-body shapes vary.
problems.fix: Say that the depicted neurons have star-shaped cell bodies. State the general structural description in terms of soma, dendrites, and axon without requiring a universal soma shape.

problems.problem: This edge places the whole stratified-epithelium concept inside glandular epithelium. Only selected stratified epithelia line particular gland ducts, and duct lining is not equivalent to secretory glandular epithelium.
problems.fix: Replace the edge with a narrowly scoped association explaining that stratified cuboidal and some stratified columnar epithelia line certain exocrine ducts. Distinguish duct lining from the secretory glandular epithelium described in C03.

problems.problem: The edge says smooth muscle is located in simple epithelium. The note actually describes two different tissues occupying different parts of the digestive-tract wall.
problems.fix: Replace located_in with a co-occurrence or functional-association relation: simple columnar epithelium lines much of the digestive tract, while smooth muscle in its wall produces movement.

problems.problem: C12 is a concept about blood cells, but the relation treats those cells as a type of connective tissue. Blood is the tissue; RBCs, WBCs, and platelets are its formed elements.
problems.fix: Either rename and expand C12 as blood tissue with its cellular components, or use a component relation and explicitly distinguish blood from its cells and cell fragments.

notes.about: This unit maps the chapter on animal tissues from pages 3 and 7. It covers the four basic tissue types, epithelial tissue (general features, glandular epithelium, Fig. 6.9 and a six-row location–structure–function table), a three-way muscle comparison table, the five panels of Fig. 6.10 on connective tissues, and a neuron diagram showing how an impulse passes across synapses.
key_questions: What are the four basic animal tissues, and what is the one-line function of each (book)?
Why are epithelial cells tightly packed with almost no intercellular space, and what does the basement membrane do?
How do simple and stratified epithelia differ, and where is each of the six sub-types located (book table)?
Why is simple squamous epithelium found in alveoli, capillaries and Bowman's capsule, while stratified squamous lines the mouth and vagina?
How should the book's broad 'often ciliated' columnar statement be clarified (ciliated vs microvilli-bearing vs pseudostratified)?
How do skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle differ in location, function, striations, nuclei and control?
What does each Fig. 6.10 panel show: blood and its formed elements, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue, adipose tissue?
In what direction does a signal travel through a neuron and across a synapse to the next neuron?

output.chapter_summary: (Outside) A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a common function. (Book) Our body has mainly four tissue types: epithelial (covering or lining), muscular (movement), neural (responds to stimuli) and connective (supports, links and cushions). Epithelium covers most organs and cavities and forms a barrier that keeps body systems separate. Its cells are tightly packed in a continuous sheet with little cementing material and almost no intercellular space, and rest on an extracellular fibrous basement membrane. Some epithelial cells become gland cells, and inward folding forms multicellular glands (glandular epithelium). The book's table lists six epithelia, each with a location, structure and function: simple squamous, simple cuboidal and simple columnar, and stratified squamous, stratified cuboidal and stratified columnar. Muscle is of three types. Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate (eccentric nuclei) and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striated, has one central nucleus and is involuntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is unstriated, has one central nucleus and is involuntary. Fig. 6.10 shows connective tissues: blood cells (five WBC types, platelets, RBC), compact bone (Haversian canal with blood vessels and nerve fibres; canaliculi with osteocyte processes), hyaline cartilage (chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix), areolar tissue (fibroblast, collagen and reticular fibres, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell) and adipose tissue (adipocytes with fat droplets). A neuron diagram shows a signal passing from dendrites to the cell body, along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips, and across a synapse to the dendrites of the next neuron.

concepts.name: Four basic types of animal tissue
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Our body has mainly four tissue types, each defined by one job. Epithelial tissue provides covering or lining. Muscular tissue helps in movement. Neural tissue responds to stimuli. Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. (Teaching tip) Use 'cover, move, respond, support' as the anchor; every later detail in the chapter is a sub-type or feature of one of these four.

concepts.name: General features of epithelial tissue
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body and forms a barrier that keeps different body systems separate. Its cells are tightly packed into a continuous sheet, with only a small amount of cementing material and almost no intercellular spaces. All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane. (Outside) Close packing and cell junctions make epithelium a selective barrier that restricts uncontrolled passage between cells. How much passes between cells varies from one epithelium to another, so it is not a complete seal. Epithelium usually has no blood vessels of its own and receives nutrients by diffusion from the tissue beneath the basement membrane.

concepts.name: Glandular epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward, and a multicellular gland is formed. This is glandular epithelium. (Outside) A mucus-secreting goblet cell is a single-cell (unicellular) gland. Sweat and salivary glands are multicellular glands formed by such infolding. Their secretory cells are glandular epithelium, while their ducts are lined by other epithelia (see C06).

concepts.name: Shapes of epithelial cells (Fig. 6.9)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, Fig. 6.9) (a) Squamous is a single thin layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries. (b) Stratified squamous is a thick block of many layers with flatter cells at the top. (c) Cuboidal is a single layer of cube-like cells with round nuclei. (d) Columnar (ciliated) is a single layer of tall cells with hair-like cilia on the free surface. Each sheet rests on an unlabelled blue base. The figure does not name it; it may represent the basement membrane described in C02 or the underlying tissue. (Outside) Naming rule: shape (squamous = flat; cuboidal = roughly as tall as wide; columnar = clearly taller than wide) plus layers (simple = one layer; stratified = many layers).

concepts.name: Simple epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Simple squamous is a single layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries. It lines blood vessels, capillaries, the air sacs of the lungs and Bowman's capsule of the kidney, and serves transport by diffusion where minimal protection is required. Simple cuboidal is described in the table as a single layer of 'short cylindrical cells'. It lines kidney tubules and glandular ducts, may have microvilli as in the proximal convoluted tubule, and does absorption and secretion. Simple columnar is a single layer of tall, slender cells, 'often ciliated'. It lines the digestive tract and upper respiratory tract, and does protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction. (Outside) A thin single layer gives a short diffusion distance, which suits gas exchange and filtration. Cuboidal cells are roughly as tall as they are wide, shorter than columnar cells. Microvilli are non-motile folds that increase surface area for absorption, while motile cilia beat to move material such as mucus in one direction. Absorptive columnar cells of the intestine bear microvilli, not cilia. Ciliated columnar cells occur in places such as the uterine tube. Much of the conducting respiratory lining (trachea, bronchi) is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

concepts.name: Stratified epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Stratified squamous lines the mouth and vagina and is made of several layers that are continuously sloughed off and regenerated. The lower layer is columnar and metabolically active, and older cells are pushed upward and become flat. Its function is protection. Stratified cuboidal is found in mammary, sweat and salivary glands. Its upper layer is cuboid, while the other layers may be cuboidal or other types, and it protects the ducts of various glands. Stratified columnar is found in the male urethra and the lobar ducts of salivary glands. It has a layer of columnar cells lying on squamous, columnar or cuboidal cells, and does protection and secretion. (Outside) A stratified epithelium is named by the shape of its top (superficial) layer, which is why the deeper cells may differ, as the book notes. Many layers and constant renewal let it withstand wear such as friction from food in the mouth.

concepts.name: Three types of muscular tissue – comparison table
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) The table compares skeletal, cardiac and visceral (smooth) muscle by location, function, appearance and control, with a cell drawing for each. Skeletal is a cylindrical striped fibre with several nuclei at the edge. Cardiac cells are branched, striped and interlinked. Smooth muscle is a spindle-shaped cell with one central nucleus. (Teaching tip) Striations occur in skeletal and cardiac muscle; voluntary control occurs only in skeletal muscle.

concepts.name: Skeletal muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: skeleton. Function: movement, heat and posture. Appearance: striated, multinucleated with eccentric nuclei, fibres parallel. Control: voluntary. (Outside) Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and move them at joints. Shivering is rapid skeletal muscle contraction that produces heat. Each fibre forms by the fusion of many cells, which is why it has many nuclei.

concepts.name: Cardiac muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: heart. Function: pump blood continuously. Appearance: striated, one central nucleus. Control: involuntary. The table drawing (p007-i2) shows branched, interlinked cells. (Outside) Electrical coupling through gap junctions at the junctions between cells (intercalated discs) helps coordinate contraction. The atria and ventricles contract in an organised sequence, not all at once. (Exam tip) Cardiac muscle is the classic odd one out: striated yet involuntary.

concepts.name: Visceral (smooth) muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels. Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and erection of hairs. Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus (spindle-shaped cell in the drawing). Control: involuntary. (Outside) Smooth muscle in vessel walls narrows or widens vessels and so changes blood pressure. Iris muscles change pupil size. Tiny arrector pili muscles raise hairs ('goosebumps'). Uterine smooth muscle contracts during childbirth.

concepts.name: Connective tissues – overview of Fig. 6.10
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. Fig. 6.10 shows (a) types of blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue and (e) adipose tissue. (Outside) Unlike epithelium, connective tissue cells are usually scattered in an extracellular matrix of ground substance and fibres. The matrix may be fluid (plasma in blood), hard (bone), firm but flexible (cartilage) or loose (areolar).

concepts.name: Blood tissue and its formed elements (Fig. 6.10a)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Panel (a) shows the cells of blood. Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte), eosinophil and basophil are drawn with a granular cytoplasm and a dark-stained nucleus. Lymphocyte and monocyte are the other white blood corpuscles. Platelets are small fragments, and the red blood corpuscle is a pale round disc. (Outside) Blood is the tissue: a fluid connective tissue in which RBCs, WBCs and platelets (the formed elements) are suspended in plasma. Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils are called granulocytes; lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes. WBCs defend against infection, platelets (cell fragments) help clotting, and RBCs carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Mature mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus and are typically biconcave discs; their shape is maintained by the organisation of the membrane and its underlying cytoskeleton.

concepts.name: Compact bone (Fig. 6.10b)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Compact bone shows concentric rings around a Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels and nerve fibres. Canaliculi radiate from the bone cells and contain the slender processes of the osteocytes. (Outside) The matrix is hard and calcified, so nutrients and wastes travel through the Haversian canal and the network of canaliculi. Each ring system is called a Haversian system (osteon).

concepts.name: Hyaline cartilage (Fig. 6.10c)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Hyaline cartilage shows chondrocytes, often in pairs, lying in a clear hyaline matrix. (Outside) The matrix is firm yet flexible. Hyaline cartilage occurs at the ends of long bones, the nose, the tracheal rings and the larynx. It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.

concepts.name: Areolar tissue (Fig. 6.10d)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Areolar tissue shows thin branching reticular fibres and thick wavy collagen fibres. Its cells are a large star-shaped fibroblast, an irregular macrophage, a rounded mast cell and a plasma cell. (Outside) Fibroblasts make the fibres, macrophages engulf microbes and debris, mast cells release histamine, and plasma cells (derived from B lymphocytes) make antibodies. Areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue found beneath the skin and around organs, where it packs and defends.

concepts.name: Adipose tissue (Fig. 6.10e)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Adipose tissue is made of adipocytes. A large fat droplet fills each cell, and the small nucleus lies pressed at the cell edge. (Outside) It stores energy as fat, insulates the body under the skin and cushions organs such as the kidneys.

concepts.name: Structure of a neuron
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, diagram) Each depicted neuron has a star-shaped cell body with a dark nucleus, short branched dendrites, one long axon and branched axon tips. The dendrites of the first neuron receive the axon of the previous neuron. (Outside) In general, a neuron has a cell body (soma) containing the nucleus, dendrites that usually receive signals, and an axon that carries signals away to its terminals. The shape of the cell body varies between neurons. Neurons are the signalling cells of neural tissue (which the book says responds to stimuli).

concepts.name: Impulse transmission and the synapse
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, diagram) The signal passes from the axon of a previous neuron to the dendrites at a synapse. It then moves to the cell body, travels along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips, and crosses another synapse to the dendrites of the next neuron. A synapse is the junction between the axon tips of one neuron and the dendrites of the next. (Outside) At the usual chemical synapse, the presynaptic axon terminal releases a neurotransmitter. The neurotransmitter acts on receptors of the postsynaptic cell and can start a new electrical response there. Transmission is typically one-way because release occurs on the presynaptic side and the receptors sit on the postsynaptic side. Electrical synapses also exist, but the diagram does not cover them.

exam_focus.why: The four tissue types and their one-line functions are standard classification and matching questions.

Location–function pairs (alveoli, capillaries and Bowman's capsule for simple squamous; PCT microvilli for cuboidal; columnar linings) are frequent match-the-following questions. Learn the book's rows, and know that intestinal absorptive cells bear microvilli while much of the airway lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar (outside).
Stratified squamous in the mouth and vagina, stratified cuboidal in gland ducts, and stratified columnar in the male urethra are classic 'where found' facts with odd-one-out potential.
The three-way muscle comparison (striations, nuclei, control) is a high-yield source of statement-based questions.
Cardiac muscle is the odd one out: striated yet involuntary, with one central nucleus.
Smooth muscle locations and functions (peristalsis, pupil size, blood pressure, hair erection) appear in statement questions.
Naming the WBC types and identifying granulocytes, platelets and RBCs is common in GS science, as is 'blood is a connective tissue'.
Haversian canal contents (blood vessels and nerve fibres) and canaliculi with osteocyte processes are frequently tested structural facts.
The cells of areolar tissue (fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell) and their roles are often tested.
The definition of a synapse and the direction of an impulse (dendrite → cell body → axon → axon tips → next neuron) are standard questions.
Features such as tight packing, almost no intercellular space and the basement membrane appear in 'which statement is correct' questions.

output.chapter_summary: (Outside) A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a common function. (Book) Our body has mainly four tissue types: epithelial (covering or lining), muscular (movement), neural (responds to stimuli) and connective (supports, links and cushions). Epithelium covers most organs and cavities and forms a barrier that keeps body systems separate. Its cells are tightly packed in a continuous sheet with little cementing material and almost no intercellular space, and rest on an extracellular fibrous basement membrane. Some epithelial cells become gland cells, and inward folding forms multicellular glands (glandular epithelium). A table gives the location, structure and function of six epithelia: simple squamous, cuboidal and columnar, and stratified squamous, cuboidal and columnar. Muscle is of three types. Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate (eccentric nuclei) and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striated with one central nucleus and involuntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is unstriated with one central nucleus and involuntary. Fig. 6.10 shows connective tissues: blood cells (five WBC types, platelets, RBC); compact bone (Haversian canal with blood vessels and nerve fibres, and canaliculi with osteocyte processes); hyaline cartilage (chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix); areolar tissue (fibroblast, collagen and reticular fibres, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell); and adipose tissue (adipocytes with fat droplets). A neuron diagram shows a signal passing from the dendrites to the cell body, along the axon as an electrical signal to the axon tips, and across a synapse to the next neuron's dendrites.

concepts.name: Four basic types of animal tissue
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Our body has mainly four tissue types, each defined by one job: epithelial tissue provides covering or lining; muscular tissue helps in movement; neural tissue responds to stimuli; connective tissue supports, links and cushions. (Teaching tip) Anchor the chapter as 'cover, move, respond, support'. Every later detail is a sub-type or feature of one of these four.

concepts.name: General features of epithelial tissue
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body and forms a barrier that keeps different body systems separate. Its cells are tightly packed into a continuous sheet, with only a small amount of cementing material and almost no intercellular spaces. All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane. (Outside) Close packing and cell junctions make epithelium a selective barrier that restricts uncontrolled passage between cells. How leaky it is varies between epithelia, so it is not a complete seal. Epithelium usually has no blood vessels of its own and is nourished by diffusion from the tissue beneath the basement membrane.

concepts.name: Glandular epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward and a multicellular gland is formed; this is glandular epithelium. (Outside) A mucus-secreting goblet cell is a unicellular gland. Sweat and salivary glands are multicellular glands formed by infolding: their secretory cells are glandular epithelium, while their ducts are lined by other epithelia (see C06).

concepts.name: Shapes of epithelial cells (Fig. 6.9)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, Fig. 6.9) The figure shows four epithelia: (a) squamous, a single thin layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries; (b) stratified squamous, a thick block of many layers with flatter cells at the top; (c) cuboidal, a single layer of cube-like cells with round nuclei; (d) columnar (ciliated), a single layer of tall cells with hair-like cilia on the free surface. Each sheet rests on an unlabelled blue base. The figure does not name it; it probably represents the basement membrane of C02 or the underlying tissue. (Outside) Naming rule: combine shape (squamous = flat; cuboidal = roughly as tall as wide; columnar = clearly taller than wide) with layering (simple = one layer; stratified = many layers; pseudostratified = a single layer that only looks layered, see C05).

concepts.name: Simple epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Simple squamous is a single layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries. It lines blood vessels, capillaries, the air sacs of the lungs and Bowman's capsule of the kidney, and serves transport by diffusion where minimal protection is required. Simple cuboidal is a single layer of 'short cylindrical cells' lining kidney tubules and glandular ducts; it may have microvilli, as in the proximal convoluted tubule, and does absorption and secretion. Simple columnar is a single layer of tall, slender cells, 'often ciliated', lining the digestive tract and upper respiratory tract; its functions are protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction. (Outside, why) A thin single layer gives a short diffusion distance for gas exchange and filtration. Cuboidal cells are roughly as tall as wide, shorter than columnar cells. Microvilli are non-motile finger-like folds that increase surface area for absorption; motile cilia beat to move mucus or other material in one direction. (Outside, reading the columnar row correctly) The book groups digestive and respiratory linings in one simplified row, so do not read it as saying intestinal absorptive epithelium is ciliated. The lining of the stomach and intestine is simple columnar: intestinal absorptive cells bear microvilli (brush border), not cilia, and goblet cells among them secrete mucus. Ciliated simple columnar occurs in places such as the uterine (fallopian) tube. Much of the conducting respiratory tract (nasal cavity, trachea, bronchi) is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Pseudostratified means it looks multilayered because the nuclei lie at different heights, but it is really one layer: every cell touches the basement membrane, while not every cell reaches the free surface. Its cilia and goblet-cell mucus trap dust and sweep it upward, which is the 'movement in a specific direction' the book mentions.

concepts.name: Stratified epithelia: squamous, cuboidal, columnar
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Stratified squamous lines the mouth and vagina. It has several layers that are continuously sloughed off and regenerated: the lower layer is columnar and metabolically active, and older cells are pushed upward and become flat. Its function is protection. Stratified cuboidal is found in mammary, sweat and salivary glands. Its upper layer is cuboid and the other layers may be cuboidal or other types; it protects the ducts of various glands. Stratified columnar is found in the male urethra and the lobar ducts of salivary glands. It has a layer of columnar cells on squamous, columnar or cuboidal cells, and does protection and secretion. (Outside) A stratified epithelium is named by the shape of its top (superficial) layer, which is why its deeper cells may differ. Many layers plus constant renewal let it withstand wear, such as friction from food in the mouth. Unlike pseudostratified epithelium, its upper cells do not touch the basement membrane.

concepts.name: Three types of muscular tissue – comparison table
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) The table compares skeletal, cardiac and visceral (smooth) muscle by location, function, appearance and control, with a drawing of each. Skeletal muscle is a cylindrical striped fibre with several nuclei at the edge. Cardiac muscle has branched, striped, interlinked cells. Smooth muscle is a spindle-shaped cell with one central nucleus. (Teaching tip) Striations occur in skeletal and cardiac muscle; voluntary control occurs only in skeletal muscle.

concepts.name: Skeletal muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: skeleton. Function: movement, heat, posture. Appearance: striated, multinucleated with eccentric nuclei, fibres parallel. Control: voluntary. (Outside) Skeletal muscles attach to bones and move them at joints. Shivering is rapid skeletal muscle contraction that produces heat. Each fibre forms by the fusion of many cells, hence its many nuclei.

concepts.name: Cardiac muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: heart. Function: pump blood continuously. Appearance: striated, one central nucleus. Control: involuntary. The table drawing (p007-i2) shows branched, interlinked cells. (Outside) Gap junctions at the intercalated discs couple the cells electrically and help coordinate contraction; the atria and ventricles contract in an organised sequence. (Exam tip) Cardiac muscle is the classic odd one out: striated yet involuntary.

concepts.name: Visceral (smooth) muscle
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels. Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erection of hairs. Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus (a spindle-shaped cell in the drawing). Control: involuntary. (Outside) Smooth muscle in vessel walls narrows or widens the vessels and so changes blood pressure. Iris muscles change pupil size. The arrector pili muscles raise hairs, causing goosebumps. Uterine smooth muscle contracts during childbirth.

concepts.name: Connective tissues – overview of Fig. 6.10
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Connective tissue supports, links and cushions. Fig. 6.10 shows (a) types of blood cells, (b) compact bone, (c) hyaline cartilage, (d) areolar tissue and (e) adipose tissue. (Outside) Unlike epithelium, connective tissue cells usually lie scattered in an extracellular matrix of ground substance and fibres. The matrix may be fluid (plasma in blood), hard (bone), firm but flexible (cartilage) or loose (areolar).

concepts.name: Blood tissue and its formed elements (Fig. 6.10a)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Panel (a) shows several blood cells. Neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leucocyte), eosinophil and basophil are drawn with granular cytoplasm and a dark-stained nucleus. Lymphocyte and monocyte are the other white blood corpuscles. Platelets appear as small fragments, and the red blood corpuscle as a pale round disc. (Outside) Blood is the tissue itself: a fluid connective tissue in which RBCs, WBCs and platelets (the formed elements) float in plasma. Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils are granulocytes; lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes. WBCs defend against infection, platelets (cell fragments) help clotting, and RBCs carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Mature mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus and are typically biconcave discs. The shape is maintained by the membrane and its underlying cytoskeleton.

concepts.name: Compact bone (Fig. 6.10b)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Compact bone shows concentric rings around a Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels and nerve fibres. Canaliculi radiate from the bone cells and contain the slender processes of osteocytes. (Outside) Because the matrix is hard and calcified, nutrients and wastes move through the Haversian canal and the canalicular network. Each ring system is a Haversian system (osteon).

concepts.name: Hyaline cartilage (Fig. 6.10c)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Chondrocytes, often in pairs, lie in a clear hyaline matrix. (Outside) The matrix is firm yet flexible. Hyaline cartilage occurs at the ends of long bones and in the nose, the tracheal rings and the larynx. It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.

concepts.name: Areolar tissue (Fig. 6.10d)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Areolar tissue shows thin branching reticular fibres and thick wavy collagen fibres. Its cells are a large star-shaped fibroblast, an irregular macrophage, a rounded mast cell and a plasma cell. (Outside) Fibroblasts make the fibres. Macrophages engulf microbes and debris; circulating monocytes can enter tissues and become macrophages, especially during inflammation, but many tissue-resident macrophages arise from embryonic precursors and maintain themselves locally. Mast cells release histamine. Plasma cells, derived from B lymphocytes, make antibodies. Areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue beneath the skin and around organs, where it packs and defends.

concepts.name: Adipose tissue (Fig. 6.10e)
concepts.core_explanation: (Book) Adipose tissue consists of adipocytes. Each cell is filled by a large fat droplet, with a small nucleus pressed to the cell edge. (Outside) It stores energy as fat, insulates the body under the skin and cushions organs such as the kidneys.

concepts.name: Structure of a neuron
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, diagram) Each depicted neuron has a star-shaped cell body with a dark nucleus, short branched dendrites, one long axon and branched axon tips. The first neuron's dendrites receive the axon of the previous neuron. (Outside) In general, a neuron has a cell body (soma) containing the nucleus, dendrites that usually receive signals, and an axon that carries signals away to its terminals. The shape of the cell body varies between neurons. Neurons are the signalling cells of neural tissue, which the book says responds to stimuli.

concepts.name: Impulse transmission and the synapse
concepts.core_explanation: (Book, diagram) The signal path is: axon of the previous neuron → synapse → dendrites → cell body → along the axon as an electrical signal → axon tips → synapse → dendrites of the next neuron. A synapse is the junction between the axon tips of one neuron and the dendrites of the next. (Outside) At the usual chemical synapse, the presynaptic terminal releases a neurotransmitter, which acts on receptors of the postsynaptic cell and can trigger a new electrical response. Transmission is typically one-way because release happens on the presynaptic side and the receptors sit on the postsynaptic side. Electrical synapses also exist but are not shown here.

exam_focus.why: The four tissue types and their one-line functions are standard classification and matching questions.

Location–function pairs are frequent match-the-following questions: alveoli, capillaries and Bowman's capsule for simple squamous; PCT with microvilli for cuboidal; gut lining for columnar. Learn the book's rows together with the standard distinctions (outside). Intestinal absorptive cells are simple columnar with microvilli, not cilia. Much of the conducting airway is pseudostratified ciliated columnar, a single layer that only looks layered. Ciliated simple columnar occurs in the uterine tube. In an exam, choose the option consistent with these distinctions rather than reading the book's row as 'the intestine is ciliated'.
Classic 'where found' and odd-one-out facts: stratified squamous in the mouth and vagina, stratified cuboidal in gland ducts, and stratified columnar in the male urethra.
The three-way muscle comparison (striations, nuclei, control) is a high-yield source of statement-based questions.
Cardiac muscle is the odd one out: striated yet involuntary, with one central nucleus.
Smooth muscle locations and functions (peristalsis, pupil size, blood pressure, hair erection) appear in statement questions.
GS science commonly asks you to name the WBC types, separate granulocytes from agranulocytes, identify platelets and RBCs, and recognise blood as a connective tissue.
Haversian canal contents (blood vessels, nerve fibres) and canaliculi with osteocyte processes are frequently tested.
The cells of areolar tissue (fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell, plasma cell) and their roles are often tested.
The definition of a synapse and the impulse direction (dendrite → cell body → axon → axon tips → next neuron) are standard questions.
Tight packing, almost no intercellular space and the basement membrane appear in 'which statement is correct' questions.
